name: Zoe Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead B shift on eight injection moulding presses making car trim clips and vent housings. I check the first part after a mould change and hear when a press is running hot; press six needs its cooling fixed. A two-year technical diploma and sixteen years at Kestrel Plastics put me among the strongest leads, and the wage is about typical for this job.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who is at home, and do you use AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Tomas drives the number fourteen bus, and our school-age children Mila and Petr are thirteen and nine. We have a mortgage, about three months saved and some other plastics plants nearby. I have never used AI; I write scrap counts on paper and Agnes in quality enters them on the tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell B shift that a quieter AI story suits me. The office can stop giving speeches and fix the cooling on press six, which made bad clips twice last week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead the cell and know each mould, and the three months we have saved covers a short interruption. Tomas’s bus wage and mine meet the mortgage, though the small sprue arms already removed night posts by leaving leavers unreplaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep checking first parts after each mould change and take the scrap counts to our next union shift meeting. If a paid Saturday run is offered, I would put a fresh part of that wage against the mortgage after bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about those small arms but secure in my own lead post for now. A slow machine change still deserves a straight answer from management.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why press six?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cooling line runs unevenly and the clips warp at one corner. I would show the reject tray rather than argue about an office chart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you used AI yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, never. Agnes in quality enters my paper scrap counts into the tablet; I do not know the AI tools.

say: I would ask for **press-six cooling** instead of another office speech.
I would take **scrap counts** to our shift union meeting.
think: My **lead post** looks steady in this slower world.
Existing **sprue arms** still worry me after night posts disappeared through nonreplacement.
do: Bring **reject counts** to the union shift meeting.
Pay extra **mortgage principal** from fresh offered Saturday wages.
feel: **Uneasy** about slow automation, while her own current wages look secure.
S0.quote: A slow machine change still deserves a straight answer from management.
fieldNote: Zoe’s **lead skill** and three-month reserve support relative security in the plateau.
Her **union role** is active even without a new AI shock, and extra debt payment needs actual paid overtime.

steps.text: Keep inspecting first clips on B shift
Bring scrap counts to union shift meeting
Pay extra mortgage principal from fresh offered Saturday wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the branch that ordering software might change office jobs quickly, while new arms spread across our presses more slowly. I want staffing numbers before the next machine order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the cell could go from eight operators to four as arms become cheaper. My lead knowledge may protect me, but if management asks one lead to cover two cells, my own hours could shrink; Tomas’s bus wage cannot pay the mortgage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the branch to seek written paid training and transfer terms, and bring the next two rotas to the meeting. If my hours are cut, we would postpone the kitchen and I would apply only for posted reachable plastics work whose pay after travel covers our bills; I would request a paid, guarded explanation of any new arm before touching it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the crew and my own paid week. I can fight a bad rota with paper in my hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a screen course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI and would need an actual paid place with a person teaching at a stopped press. I would not spend evenings on an unoffered video course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who loses hours first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kasia is temporary and usually the first name left off a rota. I would ask for the whole crew list, not just my own line.

say: I would demand **written staffing numbers** before new arms arrive.
I would seek **paid transfers** through the branch.
think: Eight jobs could become **four cell places**.
My **own hours** may shrink if one lead covers two cells.
do: Bring **two rotas** to the union branch.
Postpone the **kitchen** after a real hours cut.
Apply after **paid-hour loss** for posted reachable plastics work at bill-covering net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about her own week and younger crew members.
S1.quote: I can fight a bad rota with paper in my hand.
fieldNote: Her **lead role** may delay a cut but does not guarantee a whole paid week.
Training remains a **request** until an offered paid safe place; outside work requires a posting and adequate net wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union that thinking AGI could arrive in 2028, with capable hands-on robots around 2031. Ordering changes first, but robot arms that set moulds and driverless buses would threaten both wages later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most press jobs and perhaps Tomas’s bus shifts to go when those robots work. Three months saved cannot cover a long loss of both incomes and the mortgage; I would lie awake counting school payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cancel the holiday and kitchen plans and ask both employers for written dates. If my paid shifts end, I would apply only for posted reachable work at bill-covering pay after travel; if no adequate opening appears, I would ask the lender about temporary terms and the union about wage support before arrears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed by the expected big income loss. I could organize a meeting, but I could not make a new vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you join a demonstration?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the union calls one for notice and temporary wages. I would bring the staffing list showing who lost paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mila and Petr?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would explain why the holiday is off and keep their school costs in the budget. I would not promise the mortgage is safe before the lender answers.

say: I would distinguish **2028 thinking AGI** from 2031 physical robots.
I would seek **written layoff dates** and wage support.
think: I expect **press and bus hours** to fall with capable robots.
Three **months saved** cannot cover two lost wages indefinitely.
do: Cancel **holiday and kitchen** and request dates.
Apply after **lost shifts** only for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work.
Ask **lender and union** about temporary support if no adequate job appears.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless school-bill worry.
S2.quote: I could organize a meeting, but I could not make a new vacancy.
fieldNote: Her **2028 office exposure** differs from the 2031 physical risk to presses and buses.
Job and mortgage paths depend on **real conditions**; protest requires a union call.

steps.text: Cancel holiday and kitchen plans and request written staffing dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the branch that thinking AGI in 2031 and capable press robots around 2034 leave five years to bargain. Paid retraining must begin before the last operator loses a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At forty-eight I would still have a mortgage and children in school. I expect the press cell to shrink eventually; five years gives me time to test work outside the moulding hall without gambling our three-month reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put fresh paid overtime left after bills against the mortgage and collect the branch’s staffing figures. If the college offers me a funded forklift-and-warehouse qualification with paid study time, an actual safe practical place and a posted reachable warehouse job at bill-covering net pay, I would enrol; after qualifying I would apply for that role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, but I can work through a real timetable. I have trained new operators beside a stopped press; I would want the same care as a learner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a warehouse job really suit you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would visit the posted workplace and check shift hours against school pickup. I would not take a certificate to a warehouse that is already cutting crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no funded place is offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my paid moulding shifts and look at posted local operator work if our cell loses hours. I would not pay tuition from the mortgage reserve.

say: I would seek **paid retraining** for operators before 2034 press robots reach the moulding hall.
I would take **staffing figures** to the branch.
think: My **mortgage and school costs** remain at forty-eight.
A **three-month reserve** cannot fund an uncertain course while we keep paying the mortgage.
do: Pay extra **mortgage principal** from fresh paid overtime after bills.
Enrol in **funded paid warehouse training** only with safe place and adequate posted job.
Apply after **qualification** for that reachable warehouse role.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to check a real route.
S3.quote: I have trained new operators beside a stopped press; I would want the same care as a learner.
fieldNote: Her **training condition** includes funded paid time, an offered safe place and a local vacancy at net wages sufficient for bills.
Her **fallback search** begins after cell cuts if no course is offered, and keeps current paid work meanwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the branch that thinking AGI in 2036 and capable press robots around 2039 leave time to win a proper transfer agreement. We should bargain while the plant still needs the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be fifty-three in 2036 and fifty-six when robots may handle mould changes. Mila and Petr will be adults, but I cannot assume the mortgage is cleared or that the bus route stays staffed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep leading the cell and send fresh spare wages to savings after bills. In the first year after 2036, if I am still employed, I would check real rosters against the union agreement; after a sustained cut, I would apply only for posted reachable work paying enough after travel, and ask the branch to enforce the transfer terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about a possible later wage cut but able to act while the plant still runs. The calendar gives us bargaining time, not guaranteed pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave before robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a real paid job covered our mortgage and school obligations. I would not leave a lead wage just because a forecast has a date on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask for in the agreement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A posted vacancy list, paid training places and a clear order for transfers. I would want temporary operators included, not quietly left out.

I would keep **2036 thinking AI** separate from later physical change.

A decade gives **bargaining time**, not guaranteed wages.
do: Keep **current cell shifts** and save fresh wage surplus.
Check **post-2036 rosters** only if still employed.
Apply after **sustained cuts** for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work.
feel: **Anxious** about possible later income loss, with time to bargain.
S4.quote: The calendar gives us bargaining time, not guaranteed pay.
fieldNote: Her **2026 leadership** is current, while later roster checks require continued employment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could take press and bus wages before our mortgage is smaller. Written staffing dates, paid safe training and a union-backed transfer to real posted work would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets the savings when a press runs itself. If the crew loses paid hours, somebody in an office ought to show us the figures.

headlineQuote: If the crew loses paid hours, somebody in an office ought to show us the figures.
portrait: **Zoe**, 43, leads an injection-moulding cell with a two-year technical diploma and exceptional practical knowledge of its eight presses.
Her **bus-driver partner**, two school-age children, mortgage, typical wage and three-month reserve give some room, but no long bridge.
She has **never used AI** and serves as shift union steward, pushing for paid safe instruction and written transfer terms.
Fast robots threaten **press and bus income**; slower arrival permits funded warehouse training and applications to posted adequate roles.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time before capable robots threaten press work and bus shifts around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, offered paid safe instruction and a union-backed transfer to posted bill-covering work would help.
